title: Midnight's Children
significance: It gives supernatural powers to children born at the midnight of Indian independence, and takes the way the narrator's memory gets things wrong and leaks as its organizing principle, laying national history and personal history over each other within a single sentence. It won the Booker Prize and became a reference point for postcolonial fiction in English afterward.

title: Shame
significance: Set in a country modeled on Pakistan but given a different name, it narrates, in the grammar of allegory, the circuit through which a ruling family's honor and shame convert into violence. It pairs with the Indian narrative of Midnight's Children.

title: The Satanic Verses
significance: It crosses a transformation tale of two Indian actors who have emigrated to London with a dream-narrated religious story, dealing with migration, conversion, and the splitting of identity. Its publication led directly to international controversy and death threats against the author, and it became an event repeatedly cited in free-speech debates for decades afterward.

title: Haroun and the Sea of Stories
significance: A fantasy novel for children built on the premise that the source of stories has been poisoned and a storyteller father loses his power of speech, it takes the freedom to tell stories as its very subject. It is among the shortest and most accessible of Rushdie's works.

title: The Moor's Last Sigh
significance: It narrates four generations of a spice-trading family of Cochin and Bombay overlaid with the narrator's premature aging, tracking how a city where several religions once lived mixed together hardens into sectarian politics. It is regarded as the late peak of Rushdie's India-set novels.

title: Vertigo
significance: Laying the narrator's own journey through northern Italy over the travel records of Stendhal and Kafka, this is the prose in which Sebald first tested a narration that does not distinguish other people's lives from his own movements. The method of the three books that follow begins here.

title: The Emigrants
significance: Reconstructing the lives of four people who left Germany as four separate, independent stories, it lets the narrator approach them only indirectly, through surviving relatives, diaries, and photographs. It is the work that made Sebald's name known outside the German-speaking world.

title: The Rings of Saturn
significance: Taking a walking tour of the Suffolk coast in England as its spine, this is a prose that keeps veering off into the silk industry, herring fishing, colonial violence, and the lives of writers. It effectively voided the distinction between travelogue, essay, and novel.

title: On the Natural History of Destruction
significance: Based on his Zurich lectures, this critical book argues that the experience of the Allied bombing of German cities was left unnarrated in postwar German literature. It provoked strong rebuttal in Germany when it appeared.

title: Austerlitz
significance: It narrates, using only what the narrator has been told secondhand, how a man sent to England as a child on the Kindertransport belatedly traces his own origins. It is the last novel Sebald published, months before his death.

title: A Wizard of Earthsea
significance: It establishes a magic system in which knowing a thing's true name is power itself, and sets the enemy the protagonist must defeat as a shadow he himself has released. It presents a structure for fantasy built on self-knowledge rather than a war of good against evil.

title: The Left Hand of Darkness
significance: Arranging the report of an envoy sent to a planet whose people have no fixed gender alongside myth, folktale, and journal entries, it follows through to the end the politics and kinship of a society with the variable of gender removed. It became the reference point for treating speculative fiction as a thought experiment.

title: The Dispossessed
significance: Crossing an anarchist society's physicist's journey to a capitalist planet with his earlier life across two timelines, it builds a comparative structure that sets up neither system as a finished answer.

title: The Wind's Twelve Quarters
significance: The first collection gathering her early short fiction, it includes 'The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas,' which sets up a city whose happiness is built on one child's suffering and leaves the conclusion to the reader.

title: Tehanu
significance: Returning to Earthsea after more than a decade, it reweaves the story around the labor of women and a child, in the place left by the lost power of the male wizard the first three books had centered. It is a case of an author writing back against her own series.

title: Kindred
significance: A Black woman from 1976 Los Angeles is pulled back again and again to a Maryland plantation during the era of slavery, placed in a situation where she must keep her ancestor's abuser alive to secure her ancestor's survival. It converted the time-travel device into a tool for narrating slavery as bodily experience.

title: Wild Seed
significance: It depicts a standoff, running from seventeenth-century West Africa to nineteenth-century America, between a man who lives by moving between bodies and a woman who transforms her own body at will. It is the origin of the Patternist series, which stretches the negotiation of domination and survival out across generations.

title: Dawn
significance: After a nuclear war, humanity is rescued by an alien species and offered survival on the condition of a genetic exchange. It is the first volume of the Xenogenesis trilogy, which relocates the boundary between consent and coercion into the question of reproduction.

title: Parable of the Sower
significance: In a near-future California collapsed by climate disaster and the breakdown of law and order, a girl who physically feels other people's pain keeps a journal while building the doctrine of a new community. It is read together with its sequel, Parable of the Talents.

title: Bloodchild and Other Stories
significance: A collection of stories including the title piece, each followed by an afterword written by the author herself. In her afterword, Butler explicitly denies the common reading of 'Bloodchild' as a story about slavery and offers a different reading instead.

title: The Circle Game
significance: An early poetry collection that first made Atwood known as a poet, it treats relationships through the rules of games and the metaphor of maps. It won the Governor General's Award and confirmed that her starting point was poetry, not fiction.

title: The Handmaid's Tale
significance: It narrates, through one woman's oral account, a near-future theocracy in which childbirth is requisitioned by the state, then appends a scholarly conference paper from a later era that turns even that testimony back into an edited historical record. Atwood built it under the rule of using only institutions that had actually been enforced somewhere as material.

title: Cat's Eye
significance: A painter who has returned to Toronto for a retrospective calls back the bullying among girls in her childhood, narrating the process by which memory gets repainted like a picture. It is the most frequently discussed of Atwood's non-speculative novels.

title: Alias Grace
significance: Taking as material an actual 1843 Canadian murder case and the trial record of the maid Grace Marks, it interleaves newspaper articles, letters, and testimony, and ends without settling on a fixed truth.

title: The Blind Assassin
significance: Crossing an elderly narrator's memoir, contemporary newspaper articles, and a pulp science-fiction story-within-the-story, it makes the reader assemble where the account surrounding a sister's death has been edited. It won the Booker Prize.

title: Oryx and Crake
significance: It narrates, moving back and forth through one survivor's point of view, a world ruled by biotech corporations and its aftermath following collapse. The first volume of the MaddAddam trilogy, it is the work in which Atwood extended her own rule for speculative fiction into genetic engineering.

title: White Noise
significance: It inserts a toxic chemical spill into the daily family life of a professor of Hitler studies, narrating a state in which the fear of death is managed by brand names, television voices, and new drugs. It won the National Book Award and is the work in which DeLillo's dialogue style is most concentrated.

title: Libra
significance: It reconstructs the Kennedy assassination by juxtaposing Lee Harvey Oswald's life with a fictional plot devised inside the intelligence agencies, and places within the novel a character who organizes the historical record, making the record itself an object of the narrative.

title: Mao II
significance: Taking a reclusive novelist, a photographer, a hostage, and crowds as its axes, it develops in the form of a novel the argument that terror and mass images have replaced the writer's power to narrate the world. It won the PEN/Faulkner Award.

title: Underworld
significance: Taking the home-run ball from a 1951 baseball game as its thread, it sweeps across Cold War America in reverse chronology, setting nuclear waste and garbage disposal up as the era's central metaphor. It is DeLillo's largest-scale novel.

title: Cosmopolis
significance: Compressing time into a single day in which a billionaire asset manager crosses Manhattan by limousine, it narrates the point where the speed of finance capital collides with the limits of the body. It represents the fragmentary long-form of DeLillo's later work.

title: A Pale View of Hills
significance: In his first novel, a Japanese woman living in England retraces her memories of postwar Nagasaki after her daughter's death, revealing only between the sentences that what the narrator has displaced onto someone else's story is really her own.

title: An Artist of the Floating World
significance: A memoir in which an aging painter who had collaborated with the wartime regime justifies his own career after Japan's defeat, it sets up a narrator in whom self-defense and self-deception operate within the same sentence. It was named Whitbread Book of the Year.

title: The Remains of the Day
significance: While an English country-house butler sums up his past life during a motoring trip, his own restrained professional language comes to point at the love and the political judgment he missed. It won the Booker Prize.

title: The Unconsoled
significance: It narrates, by the logic of dreams, how a pianist who has arrived in an unnamed European city fails over three days to keep his appointments. A formal experiment breaking from the restrained retrospective narration of his previous three books, it divided critical opinion sharply on publication.

title: Never Let Me Go
significance: In the form of children raised for organ donation calmly recalling their own condition, it combines a speculative setting with a restrained narrator. It is the work that showed Ishiguro's method operates just as well on top of a genre setting.

title: Klara and the Sun
significance: Setting up an artificial-intelligence robot made to be a child's companion as its narrator, it experiments with a point of view whose observation is precise but whose grasp of human society's rules is only partial. It is his first novel since winning the Nobel Prize.

title: Waiting for the Barbarians
significance: In present-tense sentences, it narrates how a magistrate in the border town of an unnamed empire, while caring for a tortured prisoner, comes to be classified as an enemy himself. It became the reference point for allegories that take on apartheid without pointing to any specific nation.

title: Life & Times of Michael K
significance: In a South Africa at civil war, a man trying to take his mother back to her home region keeps slipping out of camps and administrative systems, remaining a figure who hands his own story over to no one. It was Coetzee's first Booker Prize winner.

title: Foe
significance: It brings a female castaway onto the island of Robinson Crusoe and leaves Friday unable to speak, his tongue cut out, asking who holds the right to write whose story. It represents Coetzee's metafictional line of work.

title: Disgrace
significance: Through events undergone on his daughter's farm by a professor who has lost his position over a relationship with a student, it presents, without judgment, the shift of power and the conditions of reconciliation in post-apartheid South Africa. It was Coetzee's second Booker Prize winner.

title: Elizabeth Costello
significance: Taking as its chapters a series of lectures an aging novelist delivers on various occasions, it brings arguments about animal suffering and the responsibility of literature directly into the novel unaltered. It is the starting point of the late Coetzee form that erases the boundary between lecture and novel.
